title: America's Treasury Secretary Threatens Allies with Divine Wrath, Proving He Has No Cards
dek: Treasury Secretary Bessent portrays America as an angry god, demanding allies submit as if to Pascal's wager. Farrell sees through the editorial: the louder the threat, the more it proves America lacks the means to follow through, and allies are already hedging.
why: Offers a contrarian reading of a seemingly tough Treasury editorial: theological bluster rarely comes due, and understanding this lets you predict allies' real leverage in trade negotiations.
who: Decision-makers in cross-border business, investors watching dollar assets and tariff risks, and policy researchers trying to gauge whether allies will cave.
skip: Skip the first 4 minutes of intro and subscription pitch; start directly with Carney's speech and Bessent's editorial.

points.h: The Treasury chief casts America as an angry god
points.body: In Bessent's Financial Times editorial on 'economic D-Day,' he frames allies' choice as a Pascal's wager. Farrell's read: he's really saying you must treat America as God, appeasing this wrathful deity by any means, lest it strike you with lightning. Farrell likens it to a 17th-century Puritan sermon, retitled 'Sinners in the Hands of an Angry God,' with the sinners being the rest of the world. The problem: such pulpit-thumping usually signals a pastor losing his congregation, not strength.

points.h: The louder the shout, the softer the stick
points.body: Roosevelt's maxim was 'speak softly and carry a big stick.' Farrell says Bessent reverses it: speak bigly and carry a soft stick. The real test is China—the country most capable of supporting Iran—and Bessent won't answer whether America dares to turn its wrath on China if it keeps buying Iranian oil. Farrell believes markets and nations are betting 'no.' So the editorial reads as an empty threat: the more overblown the language, the more America seems to be bluffing at an empty table.

points.h: Flexible realism is no strategy at all
points.body: Explaining White House behavior with 'flexible realism' is just draping a cloth over chaos. Farrell says the term, unpacked, means only: America does what it wants, and other countries should adapt. What actually drives the White House isn't strategy but a scramble for attention, like Cosimo de' Medici making everyone revolve around him—except Trump does 'a stupid version': to be the center of attention, he'll make decisions that are idiotic in both the long and short term. Other countries' response is therefore to cut losses, not to keep betting.

Federalist No. 10 offered 'ambition must be made to counteract ambition': let each person's drive for power cancel the others, grinding toward a near-public-interest equilibrium. Farrell says that mechanism has been dismantled from both ends. One end is the Republican Party: internal dissent has nearly vanished, senators won't openly block even if they object, and same-party control of all three branches short-circuits the old checks. The other end is the federal bureaucracy: the Supreme Court embraces the unitary executive theory, inspectors general are fired or cowed, and career civil servants are converted to at-will employees. An utterly incompetent person sits atop the system, and errors amplify into national madness.

points.h: Rebuilding US institutions requires learning to experiment
points.body: Farrell doesn't think institutions can return to the old consensus of the early 1990s to 2015, but he doesn't see America doomed to disaster either. His hopeful example is New York Mayor Mamdani's experiment: building feedback loops between city government and the public, turning people's real troubles into policy, and using social media to show 'I'm listening and acting.' He explicitly links this to Roosevelt's 'bold, persistent experimentation': keep what works, discard what doesn't. The open question is whether America's media and political system can tolerate a politician openly saying 'this path failed, let's try another'—without that tolerance, experiments won't go far.

points.h: The more flexible, the less anyone takes you seriously
points.body: The biggest problem with flexible realism is that it destroys an asset that erodes with caprice: credibility. Farrell cites Nobel laureate Thomas Schelling: a nation's most important assets include credibility; promises and threats that can be honored are what actually work in negotiation. If you change your mind at will, if yesterday's solemn threat vanishes tomorrow, at some point no one takes you seriously. Farrell sees America in that state today: other nations still fear its capacity to harm, but no longer believe in its capacity for long-term action. His image: a drunk grandfather holding a shotgun, everyone humoring him so he doesn't fire.

points.h: America is smashing its own web with a sledgehammer
points.body: In 'Underground Empire,' Farrell and Newman's core point: globalization is a web of interdependence—supply chains stitched together by thousands of suppliers across dozens of countries, with dollar clearing as the nervous system. America built this system while reserving a 'house advantage,' threatening to sever the network to discipline others. The Trump administration isn't delicately dismantling the web; it's swinging a sledgehammer semi-randomly at various parts. Farrell's direction is clear: full decoupling would be catastrophic; nations shouldn't aim for independence but for resilience in interdependence, while major powers relearn the language of 'restraint.'

points.h: A rare-earth card punctures the myth of invincibility
points.body: On last year's 'Liberation Day,' Bessent publicly said America held all the aces and China had no cards. Weeks later, China played its rare-earth and critical-minerals card, and America suddenly realized it held a busted flush—a hand that looked fierce but never materialized. Farrell sees this as the moment that sobered the US side; since then, speeches by Marco Rubio and others reflect the recognition that China can materially harm the US economy. The US and China now live in a fragile balance where each knows 'I can hurt you badly,' but they haven't yet sat down to turn that balance into more stable rules.

terms.def: God's existence can't be proven, but believing yields higher expected value; Bessent twists it into 'submitting to America is safer.'
Controlling chokepoints in global networks to coerce others by threatening to cut off their access.

Farrell, citing Abe Newman and Stacey Goddard, describes dividing the world economy by family and networks rather than national interest.
Poker term: a hand one card short of a flush; America discovers its hand is actually worthless.
